name: Witch hazel extract
lead: Witch hazel extract is a preparation made from the bark and leaves of Hamamelis virginiana, a shrub native to eastern North America. It is best known as the astringent 'witch hazel' sold as a skin toner, a product made by distilling the plant material in dilute alcohol.[1]

Native American peoples used preparations of the bark and leaves for swellings and external inflammations, and the remedy was adopted by early settlers in New England.[1] The plant contains tannins, including a type called hamamelitannin.[1][2]
The sources reviewed contain laboratory studies of witch hazel extract, mainly antibacterial and chemical analyses, but no published human trial of its use as a skincare toner was identified.
infobox: Tannins including hamamelitannin and gallic acid[2][3]

paras: The species was described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753. Accounts cited on Wikipedia say Native Americans boiled stems into a decoction for swellings and inflammations, and that early New England settlers adopted the remedy; some commercial history statements on that page are marked as lacking citations.[1]

Witch hazel produces gallotannins, and a metabolomic analysis profiled its gallotannin content.[3] One standardised extract used in research is described as high in phenolics, about 75% of which is hamamelitannin, with traces of gallic acid.[2]
Witch hazel is described as an astringent toner botanical. Beyond this general description, the reviewed sources do not document how toners are used or what users report.

No studies found. Related laboratory research includes an in vitro study of a witch hazel extract (whISOBAX) in which it inhibited aspects of staphylococcal pathogenesis and enhanced the effect of antibiotics,[2] a study of witch hazel added to commercial cattle teat dips,[4] and a study of its prebiotic and protective effect on Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strains.[5] A 2012 laboratory study reported that a hamamelitannin was cytotoxic to colon cancer cells.[1] None of these tested witch hazel on human skin.

card.summary: The classic astringent toner botanical; lab data exist, human skin trials do not.
card.note: Toner distillates typically contain alcohol; no human skincare trials found.

quick.overview:
Witch hazel extract comes from the bark and leaves of a North American shrub and is traditionally used as an astringent toner. Native American and later settler use on swellings and inflammations is part of its history.

The published literature found is laboratory work, with no human trials of its cosmetic effect.
quick.mechanism: It is rich in tannins such as hamamelitannin. Laboratory studies report antibacterial effects of a standardised extract; how this relates to skin toning has not been tested in trials.
quick.risks: Safety data were not reviewed in the available sources. Traditional toner distillates are made with alcohol.
